2027-03-31.title: Wednesday within the Octave of Easter
readings: What I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk
Rejoice, O hearts that seek the Lord (or: Alleluia)
They recognized him in the breaking of the bread
2027-03-31.alt: Day within the Octave of Easter, kept with the rank of a solemnity. The Gloria is sung; the Easter Sequence may be sung before the Gospel acclamation; the dismissal has the double Alleluia. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-03-31.verse: When he was at the table with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.
theo: Peter and John go up to the Temple at three o'clock in the afternoon, the hour of prayer. They still pray as faithful Jews, in the Temple of their fathers. At the gate called Beautiful sits a man lame from birth, carried there every day to beg. He looks at them expecting a coin. Peter fixes his eyes on him: “Look at us.” Then he says the words that have become a motto for the Church's mission: “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.” Peter takes him by the right hand and raises him up, and at once his feet and ankles are made strong. He jumps up, stands, walks, and enters the Temple with them, “walking and leaping and praising God.” Isaiah had promised that in the day of salvation “the lame shall leap like a deer.” The risen Lord is at work through his Church. Peter has no money, but he has the name of Jesus, and that is worth more than all the gold in the Temple. The Psalm sings: “Let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice.”

The Gospel is one of the most beloved pages of the New Testament: the road to Emmaus. On the evening of Easter Sunday two disciples, one named Cleopas, are walking about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking about everything that has happened. Jesus himself comes near and walks with them, “but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.” He asks what they are discussing, and they stand still, “looking sad.” Their words are heartbreaking: “we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel.” Hope in the past tense. They even report the women's news of the empty tomb and the angels, but it has not reached their hearts. Then Jesus speaks: “Oh, how foolish you are, and how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have declared! Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things and then enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interprets to them the things about himself in all the Scriptures. Later they will say: “Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road?”

As they near the village he walks ahead as if he were going on. They urge him: “Stay with us, because it is almost evening.” He goes in. At table “he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them.” These are the same four actions as at the Last Supper and as at every Mass. “Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.” He is not gone; he is now present in a new way, in the bread broken and given. At once, though it is night, they get up and return to Jerusalem, where they hear: “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” And they tell “how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.” The road to Emmaus has the very shape of the Mass: the Lord walks with us in our sadness, explains the Scriptures in the Liturgy of the Word, makes himself known in the breaking of the bread in the Liturgy of the Eucharist, and sends us back on mission. “Breaking of the bread” was one of the first names Christians gave to the Eucharist (Acts 2:42). Every Sunday the risen Lord does for us exactly what he did at Emmaus.
conn: Three in the afternoon, the time of the evening sacrifice and prayer in the Temple (Acts 3:1). It is also the hour when Jesus died.
Probably the great bronze Nicanor Gate leading into the Court of the Women. The lame man sat outside; now he enters, walking and leaping.
In the Bible the name stands for the person and his power. Peter heals not by his own power but by the authority of the risen Lord (Acts 3:12–16).
A village about sixty stadia (about seven miles or eleven kilometres) from Jerusalem. Several places claim the site; the exact location is uncertain.

Named only here. An early tradition (Hegesippus, recorded by Eusebius) speaks of a Clopas as brother of St Joseph; John 19:25 mentions “Mary the wife of Clopas.” The identification is possible but not certain.
The saddest words in Luke 24:21. The Emmaus story is the story of hope given back.
Took, blessed, broke, gave: as at the feeding of the five thousand (Luke 9:16), the Last Supper (Luke 22:19) and every Eucharist.
An early Christian name for the Eucharist (Acts 2:42; Catechism 1329).
altar: At Emmaus the Lord was known in the breaking of the bread. At every Mass the same risen Christ takes, blesses, breaks and gives, and is truly present in the bread that is his Body.
The two disciples ran back to Jerusalem at night. Communion is never the end of the road: it sends us back to our brothers and sisters to say, the Lord is risen.
outline: Ask: have you ever walked away from Jerusalem, away from hope?

A small table at dusk, bread broken, and an empty chair.
“Stay with us, because it is almost evening.”
live: Like Peter, you may have no silver or gold; give time, a kind word or a prayer in Jesus' name to someone in need today.
Read Luke 24:13–35 slowly tonight, and ask the Lord to open the Scriptures to you.
Say before supper tonight: “Stay with us, Lord, because it is almost evening.”
If you have drifted from the Church community, take one step back this week: a Sunday Mass, a parish group, a call to the priest.
fathers: Where did the Lord wish to be recognized? In the breaking of bread. We are sure: we break bread and we recognize the Lord. He did not want to be recognized anywhere else, for the sake of us who would not see him in the flesh but would eat his flesh.

They did not know him while he spoke of the Scriptures, but they knew him when he was fed at their table. Being hospitable to the stranger, they found God. Let us love hospitality, so that we may be received into the eternal dwellings.
Peter had no gold, but he had Christ; he had no silver, but he gave what is more precious than silver: health and the name of the Lord.
magis: The names of the Eucharist, including “the Breaking of Bread.”
The Eucharist and the Emmaus meal: Word and Bread, as in every Mass.
Mane Nobiscum Domine 1–3 (St John Paul II, 2004)
“Stay with us, Lord”: the Emmaus icon of the Eucharist.
The Church has always venerated the Scriptures as she venerates the Body of the Lord, receiving the bread of life from the one table of God's word and Christ's Body.
Signs of the Kingdom: the healings that continue in the name of Jesus.
saints: Disciple of the Lord, one of the two who met him on the road to Emmaus; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 25 September.
The Octave of Easter continues: Thursday, Friday and Saturday within the Octave. 4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy). 5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March).
2027-03-31.prayer: O God, who gladden us year by year with the solemnity of the Lord's Resurrection, graciously grant that, by celebrating these present festivities, we may be worthy through them to reach eternal joys. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Stay with us, Lord, for it is almost evening. Walk with us when we are sad, open the Scriptures to us until our hearts burn, make yourself known to us in the breaking of the bread, and send us back with joy to tell our brothers and sisters that you are risen. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: Peter healed the lame man: what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus, walk.
On the road to Emmaus Jesus opened the Scriptures and the disciples' hearts burned.
They recognized him in the breaking of the bread, the Eucharist.
2027-03-31.action: Before supper tonight, pray together: “Stay with us, Lord, because it is almost evening.”
2027-03-31.question: Where in my life am I saying “we had hoped,” and how is Jesus walking with me there?
catechism: The Eucharist called “the breaking of bread.”
Christ opens our minds to understand the Scriptures.
kidsaint: Cleopas and his friend were walking home very sad because Jesus had died. A stranger walked with them and explained the Bible. At supper he broke bread, and they saw it was Jesus! Lesson: Jesus walks with us when we are sad, and we meet him at Mass.
2027-03-31.special: Wednesday within the Octave of Easter (solemnity): Gloria; the Easter Sequence may be sung; double Alleluia at the dismissal.
term: From the Greek for “leading into the mysteries”: the teaching given especially in the Easter season to help the newly baptized, and all the faithful, understand and live the sacraments. Emmaus is its model: the Lord explains the Scriptures and is known in the breaking of bread.

family.explain: Two friends of Jesus were walking home sad. A man walked with them and explained the Bible so beautifully that their hearts felt warm. They invited him for supper. When he broke the bread, they saw: it was Jesus! Then he disappeared, and they ran all the way back to tell the others.
family.intention: We pray for all who are sad or have lost hope, that Jesus may walk with them.
family.ask: Ask: “When do we meet Jesus in our family?” Before supper, invite him: Stay with us, Lord.

illus: A retired schoolteacher in Kottayam stopped going to Mass after a quarrel with the parish council. Every evening he walked alone along the canal. One Easter week a young assistant priest began walking the same path, without mentioning the Church. They talked about books, then about the Gospels. On the third evening the old man said: you make the Bible burn like it did when I was a boy. Will you say Mass in my house for my wife, who cannot walk? The priest did. The next Sunday the teacher was back in the parish.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, stay with us, for it is almost evening. Open the Scriptures to us and make yourself known to us. Alleluia. Amen.
share: I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you (Acts 3:6). What can I give in Jesus' name today?
We had hoped (Luke 24:21). What hope of mine has died, and how might Jesus be walking beside it?
They recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:35). How do I prepare to recognize him at Mass?
pm.resp: Rejoice, O hearts that seek the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that she may give Christ, not silver or gold, to the poor and the lame.
For those who have lost hope, that the risen Lord may walk with them.
For preachers, that they may open the Scriptures until hearts burn.
For those who have drifted from the Eucharist, that they may return to the breaking of bread.
For our group, that we may recognize Jesus at the altar and run to tell others.
pm.close: Father, your Son walked with the disciples and broke bread with them. Stay with us and make us witnesses of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Peter and John meet a man who has never walked in his life. He asks for a coin. Peter says: I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk (Acts 3:6). And the man goes into the Temple walking and leaping and praising God.
The Church is not rich in silver and gold; her treasure is the name of Jesus. When we give Christ, people are healed and raised up. What do you have to give today?

In the Gospel two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem, sad. They say: we had hoped (Luke 24:21). Hope in the past tense. Perhaps some of us are walking that road too, away from the Church, away from hope.

But Jesus walks with them, though they do not recognize him. He opens the Scriptures, and their hearts begin to burn. Later they say: were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road? (Luke 24:32). That is what happens when we listen to God's word.

They invite him: stay with us, because it is almost evening. At table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them, and their eyes are opened. They recognize him in the breaking of the bread. This is the Mass: the Word that sets hearts on fire, and the Bread that is the risen Lord himself.

And then they run back to Jerusalem, at night, to tell the others. That is what every Mass does to us: it sends us out. Let us ask the Lord today: stay with us, and send us to give what we have, the name of Jesus. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, two friends of Jesus were sad. Jesus walked with them, but they did not know it was him. At supper he broke the bread, and they knew: it is Jesus!
At Mass the priest breaks the bread too, and Jesus is really there. Let us say: Jesus, stay with us!

What I have I give you, hearts burning on the road, and the Lord known at table.

Slow of heart, set on fire.

points.apply: Read the Sunday Gospel before going to Mass this week, and listen for the word that sets your heart on fire.

points.h: Known in the breaking of bread
q: Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually.
Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
points.apply: At your next Communion, say silently: “Stay with me, Lord,” and then go and serve someone that same day.

concl: The risen Lord heals through his Church and walks with us in our disappointments.
He sets our hearts on fire with his word and gives himself in the breaking of the bread.
2027-03-31.resolve: Pray each evening of this Octave: “Stay with us, Lord, because it is almost evening.”
